Lymphocyte analysis (e.g., CD4 count) would be part of this workup.

2. She was born with the lesion but noticed some growth following a minor local trauma a couple of months prior to seeking medical evaluation.

4. Her medical history was unremarkable apart from an allegedly benign breast nodule resection in her teenage years.

8. Dermoscopic evaluation findings revealed a homogeneous yellow hue with no visible vascular or pigmented structures and absence of follicular ostia.
9. The lesion was firm and mildly tender to the touch and seemed adherent to the underlying bone.
10. There were no palpable lymph nodes.

13. B, Paramedian sagittal gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

7. Both eyes had normal pupillary responses, color vision, and intraocular pressures.
8. The results of an anterior chamber examination were unremarkable in each eye.
9. The results of a dilated fundus examination of both eyes revealed significant inflammation, including 1+ vitreous cell levels, marked disc edema, intraretinal hemorrhages, and extensive sheathing of the retinal venules (Figure).

2. She reported neck swelling and an occasional dry cough but no fevers, chills, trismus, headache, dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, fatigue, or rash.
3. One week prior to presentation, she visited an urgent care clinic for evaluation of pharyngitis and white exudates on her tonsils.
4. Results of a rapid strep test and heterophile antibody test (monospot) were negative.
5. A throat culture was obtained and she was prescribed amoxicillin (500 mg twice daily for 10 days) for possible group A streptococcal infection.
6. Despite taking antibiotics for 7 days, she had no improvement in her symptoms.

10. There was no axillary or inguinal adenopathy and no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.
11. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

1. A woman in her 20s was referred to the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary Neuro-Ophthalmology Service with a 2-month complaint of frequent headaches and 1 week of blurry vision in her left eye.
2. Her ocular history was significant only for refractive error.
3. Her medical history revealed systemic hypertension, depression, and obesity.
4. Her current medications included hydrochlorothiazide and fluoxetine.
5. On review of systems, she endorsed nausea as well as paresthesia in her hands.
6. Neuro-ophthalmic examination revealed visual acuities of 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS, with no pinhole improvement.
7. Color vision (Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates) was within normal limits bilaterally, although it was noted to be slightly slower in the left eye.
8. With the Amsler grid, she reported significant metamorphopsia in the left eye.
9. Pupils were symmetric with slow responses bilaterally but without afferent defects.
10. Applanation tonometry revealed pressures of 16 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS.
11. Slitlamp examination revealed no cells in the anterior chamber or the anterior vitreous in either eye.
12. Automated (Humphrey) visual field testing revealed enlargement of the blind spot in the right eye (mean deviation, −2.91 dB) and generalized, nonspecific depression in the left eye (mean deviation, −3.41 dB).
13. Examination of her fundus was notable for bilateral optic disc swelling (Frisén grade 2 in each eye) as well as unilateral macular exudates, subretinal fluid, and subretinal hemorrhages in the left eye (Figure 1).
14. Results from brain magnetic resonance imaging with magnetic resonance venography with and without contrast were normal.

2. After recovering from anesthesia in the postanesthesia care unit, he experienced headache, facial numbness, inability to open both his eyes, and inability to move both eyes in any direction.

7. The mass also extended posteriorly and deformed the anterior aspect of the pons (not shown).  
8. After symptom onset, the mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (not shown).  
9. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis.

16. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing.  
17. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia.

14. A slitlamp examination revealed mild diffuse vasodilation and temporal chemosis, clear corneas, shallow anterior chambers, and clear lenses in both eyes.
15. A gonioscopic examination showed no angle structures in either eye.
16. Results of an undilated fundus examination was unremarkable.
17. Figure 1 shows ultrasonographic images of his eyes.Images on initial presentation.
18. A, B-scan on initial presentation showed no masses and shallow choroidal effusion.
19. B, Transsectional view of the ciliary processes on ultrasound biomicroscopy showed edema of the ciliary body and anterior uveal effusion (arrowhead).

Patient_Profile:
1. A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities.
2. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent.
3. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects.
4. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers.
5. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve.
6. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions.
7. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus hemolyticus.
8. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement.
9. Thus, he was transferred to our facility.
10. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm.
11. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts.
12. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative.
13. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively.
14. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A).
15. Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors.
16. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.A, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows polymorphonuclear neutrophils admixed with scattered histiocytes and vasculatures with a prominent endothelial lining.
17. B, Immunohistochemical staining shows myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils peripherally and in aggregates.

1. A man in his 20s presented with rapidly growing, severely painful oral lesions on the left hard palate of 2 months’ duration.
2. His medical history was significant for Philadelphia chromosome-negative B-cell acute lymphocytic leukemia refractory to multiple treatments, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, with transformation to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) status posttreatment.
3. At the time of evaluation, he had been hospitalized for 5 months with severe protein-calorie malnutrition, pancytopenia, and recurrent neutropenic fevers.
4. The patient was febrile (38.3°C), with a white blood cell count of 0.5/μL (absolute neutrophil count 0.00; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001), hemoglobin levels of 7.6g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), hematocrit 21%, and platelet count 9/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 1.0).
5. He was not receiving active cancer treatment.
6. He appeared cachectic and pale.
7. Intraoral examination revealed poor oral hygiene.
8. The left hard palate exhibited a large swelling with a 5×3-cm indurated area of ulceration, central necrosis, and desquamation (Figure, A).
9. The patient was treated palliatively with dexamethasone solution and nystatin rinse.
10. A biopsy was not recommended owing to medical instability.
11. However, the patient retained a sloughed fragment of the affected tissue, which was submitted for histologic evaluation.
12. A maxillofacial computed tomography (CT) scan completed the etiological investigation.A, The left hard palate shows enlargement with a large, focal, necrotic lesion.
13. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of palatal tissue (original magnification ×1000).
14. C, Grocott methenamine silver stain of palatal tissue (original magnification ×1000).
15. D, Computed tomographic image of the maxillofacial complex shows tissue enlargement in the left hard palate and maxillary sinus.

6. Visual acuity was 20/200 OD and no light perception OS.
7. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable in the right eye and revealed phthisis bulbi of the left eye.
8. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed prominent, engorged, and tortuous vessels with traction extending from the optic disc to the superior peripheral retina.
9. There was an associated thick fibrotic epiretinal membrane extending from the macula to the superior peripheral retina.
10. The retinal arterioles were attenuated and there was thickening of the macula with subretinal fluid found on optical coherence tomography.
11. In the superior retinal periphery, there was an orange, round, circumscribed mass with overlying tractional retinal detachment and numerous other smaller orange masses (Figure 1A).
12. Fluorescein angiography of her right eye showed early hyperfluorescence of the lesions with late leakage (Figure 1B).

14. Associated engorged and tortuous vessels emanate from the optic disc.

9. A, Hyperpigmented reticulated patches with central hypopigmentation on the right axilla.
10. B, Lesional punch biopsy specimen obtained from the right flank (hematoxylin-eosin stain).
11. C and D, Immunohistochemical analysis (positivity stain, original magnification ×100).

Patient_Profile:
1. A 25-year-old woman with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC) presented to the emergency department with lower abdominal pain.
2. She received a diagnosis of UC 6 years earlier and has taken mesalamine to control UC.
3. She was discharged a week before this admission for a UC flare that was managed with prednisone.
4. Review of systems was notable for diarrhea; however, she denied hematochezia, melena, emesis, fevers, or changes in urination.
5. Her last colonoscopy was 3 years ago, and UC without evidence of dysplasia was confirmed.
6. Otherwise, her medical history was unremarkable.
7. Family history was negative for inflammatory bowel diseases and gastrointestinal malignancies.
8. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs.
9. Her abdomen was tender to palpation in the left lower quadrant, which was soft and nondistended.
10. The patient’s complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic panel results were unremarkable.
11. Computed tomographic scan of the abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a thickened colon from the middescending colon to the rectosigmoid.
12. There was also a 2.7-cm intramural abscess in the descending colon.
13. She started receiving piperacillin/tazobactam but began to have increased abdominal pain, emesis, and inability to tolerate oral intake.
14. A repeated computed tomographic scan performed 4 days after the original scan demonstrated that the intramural mass had increased to 3.5 cm and was partially obstructing the descending colon.
15. She underwent a colonoscopy, which demonstrated multiple areas of inflammation in the rectum through the descending colon (Figure 1).

Patient_Profile:
1. A man in his early 70s with 2 months of progressive dimming of his vision was referred for evaluation.
2. He initially presented to his primary care physician reporting unintentional weight loss, fevers, and subacute visual decline.
3. Subsequent ophthalmic examination revealed mild anterior and posterior inflammation, raising suspicion for panuveitis.
4. Results of laboratory tests for sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, and syphilis were negative.
5. However, a right upper lobe lung mass noted on the chest radiograph proved to be T2N2M0 stage III non–small-cell lung cancer on biopsy.
6. On presentation to us, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/150 OD and 20/200 OS, but improved to 20/70 OU with pinhole.
7. He was pseudophakic with bilateral mild anterior chamber inflammation, moderate vitreous haze, and inferior vitreous condensations.
8. The posterior pole demonstrated bilateral diffuse retinal pigment epithelial alterations with a prominent leopard spot pattern and focal choroidal pigmented lesions.
9. Macular subretinal fluid tracked to the inferior periphery in both eyes (Figure 1A).
10. Optical coherence tomography confirmed bilateral subretinal fluid and retinal pigment epithelial irregularity (Figure 1B); nummular hypoautofluorescent lesions were interspersed within areas of hyperautofluorescence on autofluorescence imaging.
11. The optic disc and peripheral vasculature leaked on fluorescein angiography.
12. B-scan ultrasonography also showed diffuse choroidal thickening with focal choroidal thickening consistent with the pigmented choroidal lesions.
13. Ultrasonographic biomicroscopy revealed ciliary cysts associated with anterior thickening of both ciliary bodies.
14. A, Optos photograph of the left eye demonstrating diffuse retinal pigment epithelial alterations in a leopard spot pattern (white arrowhead) and focal choroidal pigmented lesions, as well as subretinal fluid that tracks to the inferior periphery.
15. B, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula of the left eye demonstrating subretinal fluid (asterisk) with areas of retinal pigment epithelium loss (yellow arrowhead) and irregular thickening (white arrowhead).
16. Pars plana vitrectomy with drainage of subretinal fluid

Patient_Profile:
1. A 40-year-old man of Scandinavian descent presented with enlarging, nonpainful upper extremity nodules developing over the preceding 9 months (Figure, A).
2. He was renovating a commercial cannabis grow-house in California at time of onset.
3. He described the construction site as being filled with intoxicating mold.
4. He reported shortness of breath and a 20-pound weight loss.
5. He denied recent travel or aquarium exposure.
6. Most concerning was the inability to use his right upper extremity.
7. Also, he developed a pathological fracture of his right foot (Figure, B).
8. Clinical examination of his forearms revealed several yam-size (4-6 cm), nontender, nonulcerated, boggy subcutaneous nodules in a sporotrichoid pattern and large nodules scattered on his trunk and abdomen.
9. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy or lower extremity lesions.
10. His medical history is significant for diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism.
11. Medications included glipizide, metformin, and levothyroxine.A, Nodules are 4 to 6 cm in diameter on the right upper extremity.
12. B, A pathological fracture on the fifth metatarsal on the right foot is indicated by the white arrowhead.
13. C, Histopathology shows pale, nodular aggregations of inflammatory cells in the deep dermis, extending into the fibrotic subcutis, as well as (D) aggregations composed of epitheliod histiocytes with few other inflammatory cells, so called “naked granulomas.”The patient’s laboratory tests showed fasting glucose of 122.0 mg/dL (reference range, 65.0-115.0 mg/dL); total calcium, 10.2 mg/dL (reference range, 8.5-10.5 mg/dL); blood urea nitrogen, 16.0 mg/dL (reference range, 10.0-24.0 mg/dL); creatinine, 1.30 mg/dL (reference range, 0.6-1.3 mg/dL); hemoglobin A1c, 6.7 (reference range, 4.0-6.0); 1,25-OH vitamin D 70, ng/mL (reference range, 15.9-55.6).Liver enzymes were within normal limits along with a negative purified protein derivative and quantiferon test results.
14. A culture from a cutaneous nodule with microbial stains for bacteria, fungal culture, and acid-fast bacilli was negative.
15. Computed tomography of the chest revealed hilar lymphadenopathy.
16. An incisional biopsy of a nodule on the right wrist was obtained, which showed nodular aggregations of epithelioid histiocytes with sparse peripheral lymphocytes, extending from the deep dermis into the subcutis (Figure C and D).

1. A 64-year-old woman with borderline resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma and a history of hormone receptor–positive left-sided breast cancer (treated with lumpectomy and radiation in 2014) was transferred to our hospital for management of a displaced percutaneous hepatobiliary drain.  
2. She was diagnosed as having pancreatic adenocarcinoma in September 2019 after developing right upper quadrant pain and jaundice, which prompted imaging and a subsequent endoscopic biopsy of a pancreatic head mass.  
3. She established oncologic care in Kentucky and received 1 dose of gemcitabine plus nanoparticle albumin-bound (nab)–paclitaxel in early October 2019.  
4. Her posttreatment course was complicated by elevated levels of transaminases, significant fatigue, and an infusion port thrombosis.  
5. Her infusion port (right sided) was subsequently removed, and she was given 1.5 mg/kg of enoxaparin daily for anticoagulation.  
6. After her transfer, the oncology department was consulted regarding treatment options for her pancreatic cancer.  
7. Several hypodense lesions in the apex of her heart were appreciated on review of her previous chest computed tomography scan (Figure 1A).  
8. A subsequent transthoracic echocardiogram (Figure 1B) was obtained and revealed several discrete, partially mobile frondlike masses originating from her cardiac apex.  
9. The cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery departments were consulted for input pertaining to her case.  
10. Both services requested cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for further clarification of her imaging findings.  
11. A, An axial slice from the patient’s chest computed tomography with contrast.  
12. The arrowheads denote atypical lesions in the left ventricle of the patient.  
13. B, A 4-chamber view from the patient’s transthoracic echocardiography.  
14. The arrowhead denotes the largest of the 3 frondlike masses emanating from the apex of her heart.

9. The pediatrics service planned to restart antibiotic therapy.

11. Perform conjunctival cultures on blood, chocolate, Löwenstein-Jensen, Sabouraud, and thioglycolate media before restarting antibiotic therapy.  
12. Provide reassurance that the diagnosis is typically self-limited.

1. A man in his 30s presented with a 5-day history of vomiting, followed by lethargy and confusion.
2. Two years prior, he was hospitalized with coma with no identifiable precipitant and an extensive workup done at that time only revealed an elevated ammonia level of 233 µg/dL (to convert to µmol/L, multiply by 0.714); etiology remained unclear but he improved with lactulose.
3. Prior to this admission, he was working in a restaurant, did not ingest any drugs or mushrooms, and had no operations and no family history of similar problems.
4. He was found to have hyperammonemia to 239.5 µg/dL and respiratory alkalosis (pH level, 7.482; partial pressure of carbon dioxide, 27.3 mm Hg, and partial pressure of oxygen, 109 mm Hg [to convert to kPa, multiply by 0.133]; and bicarbonate, 20.2 mEq/L [to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 1]).
5. Liver and kidney function were normal (protein, 6.4 g/dL, and albumin, 3.4 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]; direct bilirubin, 0.1 mg/dL, and indirect bilirubin, 0.8 mg/dL [to convert to µmol/L, multiply by 17.104]; alkaline phosphatase, 38 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase, 22 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase, 42 U/L [to convert to µkat/L, mutiply by 0.0167]).
6. His mental status rapidly declined despite treatment with lactulose, necessitating intubation.
7. Head computed tomography and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unrevealing.
8. Ammonia levels progressively increased to 1120.5 µg/dL, requiring hemodialysis and sodium phenylbutyrate, which did not lead to significant clinical improvement.
9. On hospital day 6, he developed continuous myoclonus due to status epilepticus (Figure 1A), which was refractory to treatment with lorazepam and levetiracetam as well as continuous midazolam, lorazepam, and propofol infusions.
10. Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids were requested.
11. Continuous venovenous filtration hemodialysis and carnitine treatment were started because of concern for inborn errors of metabolism.
12. Within a few hours of transfer, his ammonia level peaked to 1960 µg/dL and he lost all brainstem activity due to diffuse cerebral edema (Figure 1B).
13. A, Electroencephalography (EEG) showing diffuse polyspike complexes consistent with myoclonic seizures.
14. B, Head computed tomography showing diffuse cerebral edema, obliteration of basal cisterns, and transtentorial and tonsillar herniation.

2. She was otherwise well and had no history of tuberculosis or underlying immunocompromise.
3. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/60 OS.
4. Ophthalmoscopy revealed bilateral swollen, hyperemic optic discs with multifocal yellowish choroidal lesions located at the midperiphery and posterior pole of the retina.
5. The lesions varied in size, ranging from one-fourth to twice the diameter of the optic disc.
6. Punctate areas of choroiditis were also seen along the temporal arcades (Figure 1A).
7. Results of fundus fluorescein angiography showed bilateral early hypofluorescence, with late staining and leakage from the optic discs.
8. Results of systemic examination were normal, except for coarse crepitations of the right lung.
9. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated, at 80 mm/h, as was the C-reactive protein level, at 20.2 mg/L (to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524).
10. Chest radiograph showed consolidation in the right lower zone (Figure 1B).
11. However, results of tuberculin skin test, sputum for acid-fast bacilli, and sputum culture were negative.
12. Three days after initial presentation, the patient developed acute binocular horizontal diplopia and disorientation.
13. A, Color fundus photograph revealed bilateral swollen, hyperemic optic discs with multifocal choroidal lesions.
14. B, Chest radiograph showed consolidation in the right lower zone.

4. No erythema, edema, or sclerotic skin plaque had been found on his limbs or trunk.
5. No Raynaud phenomenon had occurred.
6. His medical and family histories were unremarkable.
7. On examination, he showed bilateral limited mobility of interphalangeal (hands), metacarpophalangeal, wrist, interphalangeal (feet), metatarsophalangeal, and ankle joints (Video).

9. The prayer sign (Figure 1A) and the “groove sign” (Figure 1B) were observed.
10. 11. Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase level, electrolyte level, thyroid function, globulin concentration, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) level were unremarkable.
12. Electrocardiogram, cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging, and plain radiographs of hands, wrists, feet, and ankles were normal.
13. Nerve conduction studies performed in all 4 limbs were normal.
14. Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activities in muscles of limbs, including fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves (1+ or 2+).

2. Three years prior, she was diagnosed with a solitary HCC and underwent surgical resection with curative intent.
3. Pathology revealed poorly differentiated HCC, 16 cm in largest dimension, with large vein involvement (T3bNXM0, R0 resection).
4. The patient underwent expectant observation.
5. One and a half years prior to the current presentation, laboratory results revealed an elevated α-fetoprotein (AFP), and cross-sectional imaging revealed multiple lung nodules consistent with metastases.
6. She was treated with nivolumab every other week and attained a biochemical (baseline, 212.2 ng/dL; best response, 3.3 ng/dL) and radiographic complete response.In the current presentation, the patient reported nonradiating epigastric pain of moderate intensity for 1 month.
7. Associated symptoms included nausea, anorexia, and water brash without emesis.
8. Review of systems was positive for unchanged chronic abdominal bloating and negative for other constitutional or gastrointestinal symptoms.
9. Laboratory results, including liver function tests, amylase, lipase, and AFP, were within normal limits, and hepatitis B virus polymerase chain reaction was undetectable.
10. Computed tomography with multiphasic liver protocol showed new enlarged mesenteric nodes and diffuse thickening of the gastric body (Figure, A).
11. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) identified diffuse inflammation and ulcerations in the gastric body and antrum (Figure, B).
12. Biopsy specimens showed chronic and active mixed inflammatory infiltrate, including intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Figure, C).
13. No overt viral cytopathic effects were observed, and immunostaining results for Helicobacter pylori, cytomegalovirus, and adenovirus were negative.A, Coronal view of restaging computed tomography of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 5-year-old girl was referred to a pediatric gastroenterology clinic for chronic constipation and poor weight gain.  
2. During her first week of life, she developed diarrhea and vomiting.  
3. With initiation of solid food, she developed laxative-dependent constipation.  
4. She underwent newborn genetic screening before routine cystic fibrosis (CF) screening.  
5. Results were normal.  
6. At the time of presentation to the gastroenterology clinic, she had no respiratory symptoms.  
7. Results of anorectal manometry, spinal magnetic resonance imaging, and thyroid studies were normal.  
8. Family history included constipation in a sister and a great aunt with CF.  
9. Her body mass index (BMI) was below the third percentile (eFigureA in the Supplement).  
10. Physical examination findings were unremarkable, including normal respiratory examination.  
11. Fecal elastase level was within reference range (>500 μg/g); abdominal computed tomographic image revealed a dilated, tortuous sigmoid colon; and full-thickness rectal biopsy was negative for Hirschsprung disease.  
12. She was referred for sweat chloride testing to assess for CF.  
13. Results of 3 separate sweat chloride tests were indeterminate (Table), prompting pulmonology referral.  
14. A 97-mutation CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) analysis panel was negative.  
15. Whole-genome sequence analysis revealed 1 CF-causing mutation (c.2249C>T) and 2 likely benign variants (c.1408A>G and c.2562T>G).  
16. No further testing; the patient does not have CF

10. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained from a violaceous plaque (Figure, C).

13. A quiet, grade II/VI systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border without radiation.
14. Her lungs are clear.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 21-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of progressive depression, bradyphrenia, dyscalculia, and fatigue, necessitating withdrawal from college.
2. She had an ovarian cyst, but her medical history was otherwise unremarkable.
3. There was no history of recreational drug use, tobacco or alcohol consumption, or sexually transmitted diseases.
4. Her mother had died at 32 years of age, after having a chronic neuropsychiatric illness, culminating in a rapidly progressive dementia.
5. A postmortem brain examination reported the presence of multitudinous corpora amylacea, but no specific neuropathological diagnosis was made.Neurologic examination of the patient during the initial consultation revealed a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 24 of 30 (points were missed on attention, calculation, and abstraction), and the patient was abulic, but it was otherwise unremarkable.
6. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed scattered small foci of T2 hyperintensity in the white matter affecting the corpus callosum, bifrontal, and biparietal regions, associated with bifrontal and bitemporal atrophy (Figure1A).
7. No lesions were identified in the cerebellum or brainstem.
8. There was no abnormal enhancement.
9. Laboratory investigations including complete blood cell count with differential; electrolytes; liver, renal, and thyroid function tests; vitamin B12 and folate levels; vitamin E; cholesterol and triglycerides; amino acids (serum and urine); syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serologies; a paraneoplastic panel; and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were unrevealing.
10. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a slight protein elevation, but no pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands, or elevated immunoglobulin G synthesis rate.
11. Arylsulfatase activity was normal.A, Axial T2 sequence showing bifrontal cerebral convexity sulcal enlargement greater than expected for patient's age, punctate bifrontal subcortical fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintense foci (right greater than left) are noted.
12. B, Brain magnetic resonance imaging axial and coronal T2 FLAIR sequence showing more pronounced global cerebral atrophy, progression of the subcortical FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the frontal predominant distribution, and also affecting the periventricular and deep white matter into the subcortical areas.
13. Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy

1. A preschool-age girl presented for evaluation of an asymptomatic plaque on the right lower extremity that had been present for 1 year.
2. Prior treatments included triamcinolone ointment and frankincense with no improvement.
3. A potassium hydroxide preparation had negative results for fungal elements.
4. Her medical history and family history were unremarkable.
5. An examination found a 1-cm nummular plaque with centralized micaceous scale and a smooth erythematous border on the right lateral lower leg (Figure, A).
6. A tangential-shave biopsy was performed to characterize the lesion.
7. Histopathological testing revealed an epidermis featuring elongated rete ridges, keratinocyte enlargement, and a few Civatte bodies, with overlying parakeratotic crust and neutrophilic cell debris.
8. Marked epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours and halos, both singly and in small collections (Pautrier microabscesses) were also observed (Figure, B and C).
9. Also, lymphocytes were present along the epidermal side of the dermoepidermal junction.
10. Periodic acid–Schiff stained sections failed to show fungal or yeast elements.
11. Immunohistochemical staining was markedly positive for CD3, CD5, and CD8 (Figure, D); CD4 reactivity was less robust and mainly restricted to dermal lymphocytes.
12. Also, CD20 was present in 5% of dermal lymphocytes, and CD30 showed variable staining of 5% of lymphocytes.A, Image of a solitary plaque on the right lateral lower leg.
13. B, Scanning view with hyperkeratosis, epidermal hyperplasia, and a lichenoid-like lymphoid infiltrate (hematoxylin-eosin).
14. C, Biopsy results with marked epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes (hematoxylin-eosin).
15. D, Biopsy results with robust CD8 signal (magnification ×100).

3. She has seen numerous physicians for her arthritis in the past and has tried various medications and devices, including copper bracelets from Mexico given to her by friends.

7. She currently takes aspirin approximately four times daily and ibuprofen occasionally.

9. There is moderate ulnar deviation of the fingers.
10. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities.

5. Bilateral dorsiflexion weakness was present (4 of 5).  
6. There were otherwise no motor deficits, muscle atrophy, or lateralizing neurologic abnormalities.  
7. On arrival, the patient underwent a stroke/transient ischemic attack workup.  
8. Results of a comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and a coagulation panel were within normal limits.  
9. Computed tomography angiogram demonstrated no evidence of extra or intracranial dissection.

1. A man in his 30s with an unremarkable medical and ocular history presented to his optometrist with reduced peripheral vision.  
2. The patient reported slowly progressive difficulty with night driving as well as perceiving objects in the periphery over the past 5 years.  
3. The patient was an avid basketball player and was forced to quit recently when he was unable to locate his teammates during play.  
4. He denied changes in color vision.  
5. There was no history of trauma.  
6. He did not use tobacco, alcohol, or drugs.  
7. His parents and both siblings were reportedly healthy with no history of ocular disease.  
8. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU, with no afferent pupillary defect.  
9. The Farnsworth D-15 dichotomous test results were normal in the right eye and tritan deficient in the left eye.  
10. His intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes.  
11. Refraction revealed hyperopic astigmatism in both eyes.  
12. His anterior examination results were unremarkable with no evidence of intraocular inflammation.  
13. The dilated fundus examination results showed minimal optic nerve pallor, vascular attenuation in both eyes, and a subtle area of increased pigmentation in the superior retina of the right eye only (Figure 1A).  
14. The fundus autofluorescence results showed bilateral peripheral mottled hypoautofluorescence contrasting a ring of hyperautofluorescence around the macula (Figure 1B).  
15. Automated perimetry was reliable and showed symmetrical severe bilateral field constriction with a remaining island of 6° of central vision.  
16. Right eye.  
17. A, Widefield photograph (Optos) showing vascular attenuation, with reduced vessel caliber in the macula (asterisks) and vessels sclerosis in the periphery (black arrowhead).  
18. There is a small area of hyperpigmentation in midperiphery just superior to the optic nerve (white arrowhead).  
19. B, Fundus autofluorescence image showing peripheral hypoautofluorescence, with mottling in the midperiphery (particularly nasally) contrasting a ring of hyperautofluorescence in the macula.  
20. Conduct serology testing to measure vitamins A, B1, B12, and folate Perform magnetic resonance image scan of the brain

7. Intravenous penicillin G therapy with 10 million units 3 times daily over 1 week combined with a UV-A1 phototherapy in 18 sessions with a maximum dose of 40 J/cm2 and a cumulative overall dose of 670 J/cm2 showed no effects.  
8. A punch biopsy was obtained (Figure, C and D).

1. A man in his late 60s with a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes for more than 10 years that was complicated by neuropathy and retinopathy presented with persistent chorea in the left upper extremity for about 1 month despite aggressive correction with insulin.
2. He was alert and oriented with healthy vital signs.
3. No evidence of cognitive impairments was present on bedside testing results.
4. The patient denied any recent infections and risk for human immunodefiency virus (HIV) infection.
5. Neurological examination results were significant for choreiform and hemiballistic movements involving the left upper extremity.
6. His home medications were carefully reviewed to rule out any medications that could cause chorea.
7. A review of his previous records indicated an admission to an outside facility 3 weeks beforehand with severe hyperglycemia and a hemoglobin A1c level of 14.1% (to convert to the proportion of total hemoglobin, multiply by 0.01).
8. Despite an aggressive correction of blood glucose levels and metabolic correction, his choreiform movements had remained unresolved.
9. On admission, a complete electrolyte and toxicology panel, including calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, yielded normal results.
10. The patient’s serum glucose level was 159 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555) and his hemoglobin A1c was 10.9% without ketoacidosis.
11. Test results for antinuclear antibodies, lupus anticoagulants, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.
12. Serum thyrotropin levels, liver function test results, and parathyroid hormone levels were healthy.
13. Copper studies, a peripheral smear, and a routine electroencephalogram yielded normal results.
14. A general screening for cancers yielded negative results.
15. The patient underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure), which showed a T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion.
16. Oral administration of olanzapine, 2.5 mg daily, in divided doses with careful monitoring of blood glucose levels resulted in the complete resolution of chorea.
17. Magnetic resonance imaging shows T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head (A) and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion (B).

2. He had experienced eye redness for 1 week, which resolved with use of artificial tears; a mild posterior headache; and paresthesias of the left thumb and index and middle fingers.
3. His medical history was significant for epilepsy as a child, although he had been seizure free for more than 10 years without medication.
4. He had no ocular history, was not taking any medications, and had no known drug allergies.
5. He smoked 2 to 4 packs of cigarettes per day, consumed 1 to 3 alcoholic drinks per day, and denied illicit drug use.
6. He denied recent travel, vaccinations, systemic illnesses, or influenza-like symptoms.
7. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/100 OS.
8. Amsler grid testing revealed a central scotoma in the left eye.
9. No afferent papillary defect was apparent.
10. Intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg OU.
11. Results of the external and anterior segment examinations were unremarkable, and no vitreous inflammation was noted.
12. Figure 1 shows findings of the posterior segment examination.
13. Results of the neurologic examination revealed decreased sensation to light touch, vibration, and temperature in his left upper and lower extremities.
14. A, Subretinal and retinal pigment epithelial lesions (arrowheads) are visible in the left eye.
15. B, Late staining of the macular lesion.
16. The arrowheads outline the border of the area that was hypofluorescent in the early frames (not shown).
17. The right eye showed similar findings.

Patient_Profile:
1. A man in his 20s presented with a 2-month history of vague, right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, with associated 5-kg weight loss, loss of appetite, and increasing abdominal distension.
2. He reported a small mass in the right scrotum that was evaluated 5 years previously and was reassured to be a nonmalignant lesion.
3. Physical examination was notable for a distended abdomen with a palpable left abdominal mass.
4. Testicular examination revealed an approximately 1-cm firm right spermatic cord nodule.
5. Laboratory tests showed lactate dehydrogenase levels of 818 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), with no significant β-human chorionic gonadotropin and α-fetoprotein levels.
6. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen (Figure, A and B) revealed innumerable masses throughout the abdomen and pelvis, with the largest measuring 17.5 × 14 × 14 cm and a 3.9-cm enhancing lesion in the left hepatic lobe, and a small amount of ascites.
7. Testicular sonogram disclosed a 1.5-cm right epididymal cyst.
8. Percutaneous biopsy and histologic examination of the dominant left abdominal mass revealed neoplastic cells (Figure, C) that were positive for cytokeratin, desmin but negative for S100.
9. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive for EWS-WT1 rearrangement.A, Coronal view and B, sagittal view contrast-enhanced computed tomographic imaging revealed innumerable abdominopelvic masses.
10. Blue arrowheads indicate the dominant mass and the red arrowhead indicates the liver mass.
11. C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×40).

2. Her medical history included neonatal seizures.  
3. She was initially evaluated at an outside institution and was found to have bilateral symmetric vision loss with nyctalopia.  
4. The onset of the symptoms was unknown.  
5. At that time, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/70 OU.  
6. The patient did not receive any ophthalmological care until 2 years later, when she was seen for marked vision loss and was noted to have a BCVA of light perception in both eyes.

13. Optical coherence tomography displayed decreased retinal thickness, more prominent in the inner layers, and hyper-reflective dots in the outer retinal layers.  
14. Family history included unilateral vision loss in her paternal grandmother in her late 20s.  
15. Both parents were healthy and denied consanguinity.  
16. The patient has 3 half sisters, all of whom are healthy.

13. In the left eye, the diffuse thinning suggests diffuse optic nerve injury (Heidelberg Spectralis; Heidelberg).
14. Insets show Humphrey 24-2 perimetry with minimal nonspecific defects in the right eye and a temporal scotoma in the left eye.
15. Refer to a retina specialist owing to retinal thinning Start intraocular pressure–lowering medications owing to GCL loss

1. A 32-year-old Nigerian woman presented with dull pain, pruritus, and discoloration of the dorsal aspect of both feet for 18 months.
2. Her medical history included a red blood cell transfusion as a child and 2 uncomplicated pregnancies.
3. The lesions started as small papules on the dorsal right great toe and left third toe that gradually spread across the dorsum of her feet over the following 12 months.
4. An over-the-counter antifungal ointment was unhelpful.
5. Her primary care physician completed a biopsy, diagnosed verruca plantaris, and prescribed topical salicylic acid twice daily for 4 weeks.
6. The lesions did not improve, and her foot pain worsened.
7. Subsequent treatment with topical liquid nitrogen cryotherapy was ineffective.
8. Three months after cryotherapy, the patient presented to the dermatology clinic regarding the lesions on her feet.
9. The patient stated that the lesions had been stable in size for the previous 6 months, without bleeding, discharge, or change in color.
10. She continued to have 6 of 10, dull, constant pain that was nonradiating, improved when she soaked her feet in water, and worsened with any type of topical pressure or wrapping.
11. Physical examination revealed multiple well-circumscribed, scaly plaques with cobblestone surfaces on the dorsal aspects of the forefoot and midfoot bilaterally.
12. Findings were more severe on the right and left hindfoot (Figure, left panel).
13. On serologic testing, the patient was negative for HIV and positive for hepatitis C virus (HCV).
14. A punch biopsy of the right foot lesion revealed psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, parakeratosis, eosinophils, papillary dermal inflammation, and intraepidermal necrosis (Figure, right panel).
15. Left, Dorsal aspects of bilateral forefoot and midfoot of a 32-year-old Nigerian woman.
16. Right, Punch biopsy of the patient’s right foot lesion (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40).

1. A 70-year old man with a history of soft contact lens wear presented for a general eye examination.
2. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal intraocular pressure.
3. Several giant follicles were noted on the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva, and a few smaller follicles were noted in the left inferior fornix.
4. Papillae were also noted bilaterally on the superior palpebral conjunctiva.
5. He did not report any redness or discharge but did note mildly increased irritation mainly from soft contact lens wear.
6. He had endorsed proper contact lens care and hygiene.
7. He also noted an upper respiratory tract illness 4 weeks before presentation.
8. Initially, he received a giant papillary conjunctivitis diagnosis because of soft contact lens intolerance and a recommendation to take a contact lens break.
9. Because of the papillary reaction, prednisolone acetate, 1%, twice a day for 2 weeks was prescribed.
10. After 3 months, the symptoms had improved in the left eye, but conjunctival follicles were still present in the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva (Figure 1).
11. The patient subsequently underwent testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea, and the result was negative.
12. At the 1-year follow-up, the examination findings were unchanged.
13. During this follow-up, Lyme disease and Epstein-Barr virus serologic tests were performed in addition to repeated chlamydia testing.
14. The results were negative, except for a positive Epstein-Barr virus IgG.

1. A man in his 50s presented to our dermatology department with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area.
2. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed.

4. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead.

9. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.
10. Skin biopsies were performed on the left side of the vertex and the forehead.
11. Histopathologic findings of the 2 biopsy specimens were identical (Figure, C and D).
12. A, Clinical image of annular arc from a longitudinally furrowed skin lesion on the left eyebrow and forehead to an alopecic lesion.

15. Manage medically with antihypertensive agents and a walking program.  
16. Perform angioplasty of the right renal artery and angioplasty with stenting of the right external iliac artery.  
17. Administer cilostazol for claudication and continue lisinopril for hypertension.

1. A previously healthy man in his 30s presented with spontaneous bruising, epistaxis, and haematuria.

4. Dexamethasone was prescribed to reduce the risk of ATRA syndrome, a potentially life threatening complication seen in these patients and characterized by fever, pulmonary infiltrates, hypotension, and leucocytosis.
5. After 12 days of treatment, the patient developed pyrexia and was started on empiric antibiotics.
6. Two days later he developed tender black spots on the scrotum that progressed to painful ulcers over 8 days (Figure, A).

8. Peripheral blood cultures and skin swabs from the lesions did not identify bacterial or viral infection.
9. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a subcutaneous hypervascular lesion with no abscess.
10. The development and progression of scrotal ulceration coincided with recovery in neutrophil count from 0.3 × 109/L to 1.2 × 109/L and persistent pyrexia.
11. As scrotal ulceration progressed, they enlarged and became necrotic with a black eschar.
12. A specimen was obtained for histopathology.

12. Two weeks after the initial consultation, the patient reported persistent but improved symptoms in the left eye.
13. At this follow-up visit, her visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/200 OS.

1. A 62-year-old patient presented to the ophthalmology department with sudden painless vision loss in her right eye that occurred 24 hours ago.  
2. She also reported a 4-week history of right ear pain and fullness, discomfort over her frontal and maxillary sinuses, and nasal congestion without discharge.  
3. Over the past 2 weeks, she had experienced drenching night sweats, cramps in her quadriceps, and weight loss of 3 kg.  
4. She denied respiratory symptoms, headaches, scalp tenderness, or jaw claudication.  
5. She took no regular medication and did not smoke.  
6. At presentation, her visual acuities were perception of light OD and 20/20 OS.  
7. There was a right relative afferent pupillary defect.  
8. Dilated fundus examination showed a cherry red spot in the right macula with hyperreflectivity and thickening of the inner retinal layers on optical coherence tomography (Figure 1A and B).  
9. External eye examination results and ocular motility were normal.  
10. Examination by an otolaryngologist revealed normal tympanic membranes and a dry but otherwise normal nasal mucosa on flexible endoscopy.  
11. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count, 15 000 /µL; to convert to 109 per liter, multiply by 0.001) with neutrophilia (white blood cell count, 12 500 /µL), elevated C-reactive protein (19.4 mg/dL; to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10), elevated plasma viscosity (2.06 mPas), and thrombocytosis (467 ×103/µL; to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 1).  
12. Kidney function was within normal limits.  
13. Chest radiograph results were unremarkable.  
14. False-color and red-free (inset) fundus photograph of the right eye shows retinal pallor (white arrowheads) with a cherry red spot (yellow arrowhead) in the macula (A).  
15. Optical coherence tomography of the right macula shows hyperreflectivity and thickening of the inner retinal layers (yellow arrowheads) and hyporeflectivity of the outer retinal layers (blue arrowheads), except for increased signal intensity in the outer retinal layers of the fovea (white arrowhead) (B).

1. A 60-year-old man with advanced melanoma presented with headaches and increasing fatigue during treatment with ipilimumab.
2. Several months earlier, he presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath.
3. Imaging revealed pulmonary emboli and incidental groin lymphadenopathy.
4. Biopsy of a lymph node showed melanoma.
5. He then underwent inguinal lymph node dissection and was found to have 9 lymph nodes involved with melanoma (stage IIIC melanoma).He was then treated with ipilimumab (3 mg/kg), a monoclonal antibody to cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4), every 3 weeks, as part of an investigational adjuvant therapy clinical trial.
6. When presenting for his fourth and final dose of ipilimumab, he reported central headaches, severe fatigue, poor appetite, intermittent nausea, and a mild rash.
7. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits.
8. Physical examination had largely unremarkable results except for a slightly red, raised rash over his chest and proximal extremities.Laboratory testing showed the following: thyrotropin, 0.02 mIU/L (reference range, 0.3-5.0 mIU/L), and free thyroxine, less than 0.25 ng/dL (reference range, 0.5-1.2 ng/dL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 12.871).
9. Cosyntropin stimulation test showed a cortisol peak level of 0.9 µg/dL (reference range, >20 µg/dL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 27.588).
10. He had low corticotropin (<5 pg/mL; reference range, 7-51 pg/mL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 0.22) and testosterone levels (<0.1 ng/mL; reference range, 2-11 ng/mL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 0.0347).
11. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is shown in the Figure.

12. Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%.

14. 8. Echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac chambers and valves.  
9. However, an echogenicity was noted compressing the superior vena cava and right ventricle.  
10. The patient subsequently underwent computed tomographic imaging of the chest that revealed a large, 16.2 × 6.8 × 5.6-cm anterior mediastinal mass compressing the right cardiac structures, particularly the superior vena cava.  
11. The mass consisted mostly of fat attenuation, but was interspersed with nodular densities (Figure 1B).  
12. Tumor marker levels, including α-fetoprotein, lactate dehydrogenase, and β-human chorionic gonadotropin, were within reference ranges.  
13. Chest imaging.  
14. A, Radiograph showed a convexity on the right heart border and cardiomegaly.

1. A man in his 50s with a history of ‎poorly controlled type 2 diabetes reported decreased vision in both eyes.
2. On examination, visual acuity was counting fingers OD and 20/200 OS.
3. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable.

6. He subsequently underwent vitrectomy in the right eye for nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage with an uneventful postoperative course and improvement of his visual acuity to 20/100.
7. The patient was lost to follow-up and returned 4 months later with visual acuity 20/125 OD and counting fingers OS, with a vitreous hemorrhage in the left eye for which he underwent vitrectomy with thorough panretinal photocoagulation (1200 spots).

9. The conjunctiva had mild hyperemia with foci of subconjunctival hemorrhage, the anterior chamber was deep and quiet, the anterior vitreous contained no cells, and a few cobweblike, tan strands were present throughout the vitreous cavity.
10. Topical timolol/acetazolamide and brimonidine were started twice daily, together with prednisolone acetate and moxifloxacin every 6 hours.
11. On postoperative day 3, the patient noted decreased visual acuity OS but he denied pain or discharge.
12. Visual acuity was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 17 mm Hg.
13. The anterior chamber had minimal inflammation.
14. Extensive strands and veils were noted throughout the vitreous cavity (Figure 1).
15. Anterior vitreous cavity (A) and wide-field fundus photograph (B) of the left eye demonstrating extensive transvitreal strands and sheets.

Patient_Profile:
1. A boy in his late teens with short stature presented with gradual loss of vision in both eyes since 8 years of age.  
2. He received a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes at 10 years of age and has been taking insulin since the diagnosis.  
3. He had consulted several physicians for hearing loss during the past 2 years.  
4. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics for frequent urinary tract infections.  
5. The results of a systemic examination revealed hypochondroplasia, alopecia (Figure 1), and generalized hypotonia.  
6. His best-corrected visual acuity was 6/60 OU.  
7. Bjerrum tangent screen visual field analysis showed preservation of central 10 degrees of fields.  
8. His color vision was defective, and his pupils were slow reactive to light.  
9. The results of an optic nerve examination revealed bilateral pale optic discs with no evidence of edema and normal retinal vasculature.  
10. The results of the examination of the macula were normal in both eyes, with no diabetic retinopathy.  
11. A urine specific gravity test was performed, and the urine specific gravity was found to be low (sp g 1.001-1.003), consistent with diabetes insipidus.  
12. Physical presentation of the patient, an adolescent boy presenting with hypochondroplasia, alopecia, and short stature.  
13. Order a hormone profile (thyrotropin, adrenocorticotrophic hormone, growth hormone, and testosterone) and consult endocrinology

Patient_Profile:
1. A white man in his 70s was referred for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging fleshy nodule of the right nasal conjunctiva.
2. The patient noted redness, pain, and a foreign body sensation on his right eye for 2 weeks.

4. The chest radiographic findings and blood work results were unremarkable.
5. The lack of response to oral prednisone therapy led to suspicion of a possible malignant neoplasm, and the patient was referred for our opinion.

7. Two years before referral, bladder cancer was diagnosed and was treated surgically and with multiple rounds of intravesical BCG immunotherapy.
8. The most recent BCG treatment was 5 months before presentation to the Ocular Oncology Service at Wills Eye Hospital, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
9. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/40 OS.
10. Anterior segment examination findings were remarkable for a limbal-based amelanotic lesion of the nasal conjunctiva measuring 5 mm in basal diameter and 1.5 mm thick and fed by large dilated conjunctival and episcleral vessels (Figure 1).
11. Ocular ultrasonography revealed no intraocular involvement.
12. The remainder of the eye examination was unremarkable.
13. External photograph depicting a perilimbal erythematous conjunctival nodule with dilated episcleral vessels.

1. A 65-year-old white woman with stage IV breast cancer with metastases to the lungs and liver presented with a new onset of what she called “multiple green spots” in both eyes for 3 days.
2. The spots were stationary; she denied any floaters or photopsias.
3. The onset was simultaneous in both eyes, with no associated eye pain or photophobia.
4. There was no ocular history, and a recent comprehensive eye examination had normal results.
5. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU.
6. An anterior segment examination had unremarkable results.
7. There was no vitritis, and her optic nerves were pink and sharp.
8. A dilated fundus examination revealed multifocal, hypopigmented, cream-colored spots scattered throughout the posterior pole in both eyes.
9. These spots were hyperautofluorescent on fundus autofluorescence and localized to the subretinal space (Figure 1).
10. 7. She also had a history of breast cancer in her 40s, for which she underwent lumpectomy and tamoxifen therapy.  
8. She had undergone surgical excision of a gastric polyp in her early 50s.  
9. She had no history of radiation therapy.

11. There was a 12 × 7–cm indurated pink and deep purple plaque on the right side of the abdomen, with 2 focal areas of ulceration (Figure).  
12. Extending outward from this plaque were finger-like projections of purple subcutaneous papules.  
13. Inferior to the plaque there was an approximately 3-cm, tender, orange-to-yellow patch.  
14. No lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were noted.

7. Laboratory evaluation revealed mild neutropenia and lymphopenia with normal hemoglobin and platelet counts.
8. Antinuclear antibody screening results were negative.
9. The results of a comprehensive metabolic panel, C3, C4, serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, ferritin, copper, zinc, haptoglobin, HIV, hepatitis B and C serologic tests, and rapid plasma reagin were negative.
10. Lactate dehydrogenase was mildly elevated.
11. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 41 mm/h.
12. Routine cancer screening was up to date.
13. Therapeutic trials of dapsone and dapsone in combination with colchicine were not effective.

1. A 54-year-old man presented for evaluation of new-onset pancytopenia.
2. He had a distant history of viral myocarditis and was taking lisinopril, carvedilol, furosemide, aspirin, and a multivitamin.
3. No new medications had been started in the past year.
4. Twelve years prior, he underwent uncomplicated Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery.
5. Review of systems was notable for fatigue and negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss, dyspnea, or abnormal bleeding.
6. Examination revealed temperature of 36.7°C; heart rate, 91/min; blood pressure, 120/70 mm Hg; and body mass index, 20.1 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared).
7. He was well-appearing with conjunctival pallor but no petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly, and a normal neurologic examination.
8. Laboratory evaluation showed a white blood cell count of 1.7 × 103/μL with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.17 × 103/μL; hemoglobin level, 7 g/dL with mean corpuscular volume of 103 fL (reticulocyte index, 0.94); and platelet count, 116 × 103/μL.
9. Results of a complete blood cell count from 8 months prior were normal.
10. Results of serum protein electrophoresis were normal, as were levels of lactate dehydrogenase, ferritin, folate, vitamin B12, and thyroid-stimulating hormone.
11. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed no lymphadenopathy, masses, or hepatosplenomegaly.
12. Peripheral blood smear showed occasional pseudo Pelger-Huet cells and rare teardrop cells.
13. Histopathologic examination of bone marrow aspirate revealed a normocellular marrow and dyserythropoiesis with vacuolized and dysplastic erythroid precursors (Figure, panel A), left-shifted granulocytic maturation with vacuolized granulocytic precursors, ring sideroblasts (Figure, panel B), and no increase in blasts.
14. Cytogenetic studies from the bone marrow did not reveal any abnormalities.
15. Histopathologic examination of bone marrow aspirate from patient (A, Wright-Giemsa, original magnification ×1000; B, Prussian blue iron, original magnification ×1000).

Patient_Profile:
1. A man aged 48 years was followed up for bilateral proliferative diabetic retinopathy, having previously been treated with panretinal photocoagulation as well as macular laser for diabetic macular edema (DME) in each eye several years ago.
2. The left eye had undergone pars plana vitrectomy for the repair of a macula-involving tractional retinal detachment, but despite anatomical success, visual acuity remained count fingers, presumably due to a loss of retinal tissue from macular ischemia.
3. The right eye had undergone cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation and a pars plana vitrectomy for nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage.
4. After this surgery, the patient was treated for persistent DME and received multiple intravitreous injections of bevacizumab, ranibizumab, triamcinolone acetonide, and a dexamethasone intravitreal implant, but the DME persisted, and visual acuity was 20/70 OU.
5. Therefore, a fluocinolone acetonide intravitreal implant (ILUVIEN; Alimera Sciences Inc) was injected.
6. Soon after the procedure, the patient began complaining of a large, linear “floater” in his central vision, which was very disturbing to him.
7. On examination, the implant was seen in the middle of the vitreous cavity in a vertical orientation and in the visual axis (Figure 1).
8. The patient was observed for 2 weeks with the hope the implant would settle down or move out of the visual axis, but this did not happen.
9. Optos image of the patient’s right eye.
10. The fluocinolone acetonide intravitreal implant can be seen in the middle of the vitreous cavity, very close to the visual axis.
11. Additionally, panretinal photocoagulation laser scars and a superior area of fibrosis can be seen.

16. Conjunctival swabs and eyelid vesicle fluid were taken for polymerase chain reaction testing.

1. A 55-year-old white woman presented with 1 week of decreased visual acuity and ache on abduction in the right eye.
2. She had decreased right-sided hearing and tinnitus, a moderate right-sided frontal headache, and an unsteady gait.
3. She did not have diplopia, facial numbness, or paresthesias.
4. She had a history of stage IV breast cancer treated with letrozole after a mastectomy 5 years prior.
5. On an initial examination, her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/25 OS, with dyschromatopsia, relative afferent pupillary defect, and visual-field defects on the right side.
6. Her extraocular movements were full.
7. A dilated fundus examination demonstrated a pale right optic nerve.
8. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was reported to have normal results, but on review, we noted thickening and enhancement of both optic nerves (with the right eye larger than the left eye), cranial nerve III in the right eye, cranial nerve V bilaterally, the pituitary infundibulum, and the hypothalamus, as well as adjacent cavernous sinuses.
9. Leptomeningeal thickening over the convexities of the anterior frontal lobes was also evident.
10. The patient’s cerebrospinal fluid contained a small population of polyclonal CD19+ B cells and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
11. An extensive laboratory workup, including tests for HIV, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, serum protein electrophoresis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, complete blood cell count, antiganglioside antibodies, anti–myelin-associated glycoprotein antibodies, and angiotensin-converting enzyme, gave normal results.
12. A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the thorax and a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)/CT scan revealed no abnormalities.
13. Clinically, she initially responded to corticosteroids.
14. Over the ensuing 5 years, she had multiple similar presentations that also included facial pain and paresthesias.
15. She also developed a chronic small-fiber peripheral neuropathy and was treated with mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, and intravenous immunoglobulin at various points.

1. A woman in her early 50s was admitted to the hospital with several days of headaches, bilateral photophobia, and blurry vision.
2. Her medical history was notable for cystic fibrosis, receipt of bilateral lung transplant, cytomegalovirus (CMV) viremia, and chronic kidney disease.
3. Earlier treatment for CMV viremia included valganciclovir hydrochloride therapy that was discontinued because of the development of drug resistance and foscarnet sodium therapy with resultant renal dysfunction.
4. The patient was subsequently treated with intravenous renally dosed cidofovir therapy; however, she again developed a nephrotoxic reaction and required dosage reduction in the weeks before presentation.
5. At admission, cidofovir therapy was discontinued because of acute kidney injury (creatinine level, 5.75 mg/dL) (to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4).
6. The findings of a workup for meningitis were unremarkable.
7. Ophthalmic consultation occurred 1 week after admission.
8. The patient’s visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/25 OS.
9. Pupils were minimally reactive and without an afferent pupillary defect.
10. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 12 mm Hg OS.
11. Portable slitlamp examination findings included bilateral posterior synechiae and a shallow anterior chamber in the left eye.
12. No anterior segment cell was appreciable by portable examination.
13. The patient had early nuclear sclerosis and posterior subcapsular cataracts in both eyes.
14. Results of a fundus examination demonstrated bilateral temporal choroidal elevations without vitritis, vascular sheathing, retinitis, or optic nerve abnormalities.
15. B-scan ultrasonography findings demonstrated bilateral choroidal effusions (Figure 1).
16. B-scan ultrasonographic images obtained at initial presentation demonstrating choroidal effusions in a patient with recent exposure to cidofovir.
17. Discontinue cidofovir therapy, and start therapy with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegia

2. He described increased anxiety and a pleuritic chest pain that began a few hours prior to his ED visit, but no hemoptysis.  
3. He had no personal history of cancer, venous thrombosis, recent surgery, trauma, or admission to hospital.  
4. His medications included fluoxetine, atorvastatin, vitamin D, magnesium, and niacin.  
5. On examination, his blood pressure was 164/82 mm Hg; pulse rate, 104/min; and respiratory rate, 18/min.  
6. Oxygen saturation level was 96% in room air.  
7. His lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally.  
8. No extra heart sounds or murmurs were noted.  
9. Examination of his extremities were unremarkable with no leg symptoms or swelling or pain at calf palpation.  
10. Laboratory test results showed a hemoglobin level of 160 g/dL (reference range, 14.0-17.5 g/dL), a platelet count of 129 × 103/μL (reference range, 150-350 × 103/μL), and a serum creatinine level of 1.26 mg/dL (reference range, 0.6-1.2 mg.dL) (111 μmol/L; reference range, 13-106 μmol/L).  
11. His chest film was normal.  
12. The attending physician’s presumptive diagnosis was pulmonary embolism (PE).  
13. His pretest clinical probability of PE according to the 2-level Wells score was likely (1.5 points for heart rate >100, and 3.0 for other diagnoses less likely than PE).  
14. Therefore, D-dimer measurement was not performed.  
15. His computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) result is reported in the Table.  
16. Rule out PE and perform a work up for alternative diagnoses.  
17. Obtain a bilateral lower limb veins compression ultrasonography.  
18. Obtain a lung ventilation-perfusion (V̇/Q̇) scan or pulmonary angiogram.

2. She had a history of chronic migraines and reported worsening headaches during the past 3 months.

4. She reported intermittent tinnitus but denied transient visual obscurations or hearing changes.
5. Results of a review of systems were otherwise unremarkable.
6. The patient was not taking any medications and denied a history of illicit drug use.

8. Extraocular movements were intact, and pupils were round and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect.
9. Her intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 10 mm Hg OS.

8. Fewer, scattered macules were on the face, neck, trunk, upper legs, upper arms, and scrotum.  
9. Dusky bullae were seen on the bilateral dorsal aspect of the hands, fingers, toes, and heels.  
10. In the oral cavity, there was 1 violaceous macule on the right buccal mucosa and a few linear, horizontal, white lines on the left buccal mucosa.  
11. Laboratory findings revealed a white blood cell count of 25 600/μL (reference range, 3700-10 500/μL) and a platelet count of 12 400/μL (reference range, 15 000-40 000/μL).  
12. Results from a Tzanck smear from the initial lesion on the right dorsal aspects of the third finger were negative for multinucleated giant cells.  
13. A punch biopsy was performed on the anterior side of the thigh

**Reasoning:**

1.  **Sentence 1:** Provides patient demographics and the initial complaint, setting the scene but not directly related to the legal concept. [Low Relevance]
2.  **Sentence 2:** Describes a diagnostic step taken, which is part of the clinical course but not the core legal issue. [Low Relevance]
3.  **Sentence 3:** This is the key finding – a surgical sponge left inside the patient. This is the *res* (the thing) that speaks for itself (*loquitur*). It's a classic example of negligence that is obvious without needing direct proof of *how* it happened. [High Relevance]
4.  **Sentence 4:** This sentence explicitly describes the legal situation where the plaintiff establishes that the injury (sponge left inside) could only have occurred due to negligence. This is the definition of *res ipsa loquitur* – "the thing speaks for itself," meaning the circumstances strongly imply negligence. [High Relevance]

**Explanation of Legal Concepts:**

*   **Res ipsa loquitur:** "The thing speaks for itself." This doctrine applies when (1) the event is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur in the absence of negligence, (2) it was caused by an agency or instrumentality within the exclusive control of the defendant, and (3) it was not due to any voluntary action or contribution on the part of the plaintiff. Leaving a surgical sponge inside a patient fits this definition perfectly.
*   **Collateral estoppel:** Prevents relitigation of an issue already decided in a prior case. Not relevant here.
*   **Proximate cause:** The legal cause of an injury; the injury must be a foreseeable result of the defendant's negligence. While negligence is involved, the specific legal doctrine described is *res ipsa loquitur*.
*   **Respondeat superior:** "Let the master answer." Holds an employer liable for the wrongful acts of an employee committed within the scope of employment. Not the primary concept described.

Therefore, *res ipsa loquitur* (C) is the most appropriate term. Sentences 3 and 4 directly support this conclusion.

1. A man in his 50s with diagnoses of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, hepatitis B, and latent tuberculosis presented with a slow-growing nodule on the left foot.
2. The lesion started 1 year prior as a tender red nodule on the medial aspect of his first metatarsophalangeal joint, which would enlarge and become painful approximately once a month (Figure, A).

10. C, Higher magnification highlights eosinophilic material surrounding small cocci.
11. D, Gram staining of the biopsy supported the diagnosis.

9. Findings on slitlamp examination of the anterior segment were unremarkable.  
10. A single, 1-cm, oval, lightly pigmented macule with irregular borders was noted on her right upper arm.  
11. Dilated fundus examination revealed eccentric, yellow-clear, preretinal lesions in the maculas of both eyes.  
12. Optical coherence tomography revealed hyperreflective areas on the surface of the macula with a spiculated appearance, projecting anteriorly into the vitreous.  
13. There was an increase in retinal thickness and loss of the foveal contour in both eyes (Figure).  
14. Optical coherence tomography of the right eye (A) showing an atypical epiretinal membrane with anterior projection into the vitreous and hazy borders and the left eye (B) showing a similar epiretinal membrane with mild anterior projection and hazy borders.  
15. Obtain a family medical history and genetic testing Recommend pars plana vitrectomy with epiretinal membrane peel

16. Artificial tears and ointment were initiated to treat the aqueous tear deficiency.

1. A 63-year-old white man with a history of cigarette use (≥80 pack-years) and alcohol dependence presented to the ophthalmology clinic with several weeks of left eye pain and redness.

10. The results of proteinase 3–antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing and interferon γ release assay using QuantiFERON-TB gold (QFT) (Qiagen) were positive.
11. Chest computed tomography revealed tiny, scattered solid pulmonary nodules that were too small to characterize according to the radiology department.
12. The patient was referred to the infectious diseases clinic, where the results of sputum culture and polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacteria tuberculosis were negative.
13. Pulmonology evaluation determined that the pulmonary nodules were too small for biopsy via bronchoscopy.Slitlamp photograph of the left eye shows diffuse hyperemia with dilated vessels and scleral thinning.
14. Initiate rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) therapy

11. Choroidal folds were observed 3 disc diameters temporal to the macula, extending to the periphery.

11. The peripheral retina had well-demarcated peripheral retinal whitening with scalloped margins and intraretinal hemorrhages in all quadrants (Figure 1A and B).
12. Four days later, repeat fundus photography showed that the peripheral lesions had coalesced into larger circumferential necrotic regions (Figure 1C).
13. A, Color fundus photography montage of the left eye shows hyperemic disc with blurred margins, vascular sheathing, and peripheral retinal whitening.
14. B, Magnified image of the temporal retina shows well-demarcated infiltrates with scalloped margins and adjacent intraretinal hemorrhages.
15. C, Montage from 4 days later shows convergence of necrotic lesions in a circumferential pattern around the equator with confluence in the anterior periphery.
16. Fresh laser barricade spots are seen at the posterior margin of the areas of necrosis.

Patient_Profile:
1. A Chinese woman had painless, gradually declined vision for 2 years without redness.
2. She had a medical history of vomiting and emaciation in her early 40s.
3. Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) had been done for her left eye owing to vitreous opacity half a year prior.
4. She claimed that her younger brother died of liver cancer and her mother had lost vision because of vitreous hemorrhage and glaucoma.
5. She denied any history of systemic disorders.
6. On initial examination, best-corrected visual acuity was measured at 0.1 (20/200) OU.
7. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS.
8. Her anterior segment examination results were within normal limits.
9. Dilated fundus examination demonstrated bilateral vitreous opacity without cells (Figure).
10. The peripheral residual vitreous cortex in the left eye was as cloudy as the cortex in the right eye.
11. Fundus was not visible in the right eye and was normal in the left eye.
12. A bilateral ocular ultrasonography showed normal results except for vitreous opacity.
13. The patient weighed 37.0 kg and was 155 cm tall.
14. Her blood pressure was 113/70 mm Hg.
15. Mild anemia (hemoglobin level 10.5 g/dL vs a normal range of 11.0-15.0 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) was found in routine blood test results.
16. Liver and renal functions were normal according to serum test results.
17. The results of an electronic cardiogram were negative.
18. Mosaic 9-field 50° fundus photography showed a uniform, glassy, woollike appearance of the vitreous in the right eye (A) and peripheral vitreous opacity in the left after pars plana virectomy (B).
19. Aqueous humor biopsy for cytometry and biochemical test

3. She had a 25-year history of bulimia and was purging almost daily.  
4. She reported an inability to go more than 3 days at a time without purging and noted a reduction in the pressure and size of her lesions with respite from these daily episodes.  
5. She had no history of eye surgery, hypertension, atherosclerotic disease, or other risk factors for vascular disease.  
6. The patient first noticed these lesions 15 years ago in association with a subconjunctival hemorrhage on the left side.  
7. 8. The anterior segment examination showed bilateral superior (Figure, A) and inferior (Figure, B) large dilated blood vessels underlying the palpebral conjunctivae.  
9. Complete ophthalmic and orbital examinations revealed no other abnormalities. Eyelids of the patient demonstrating vascular lesions visible within the palpebral tissue at the time of presentation.  
10. A, Atypical vascular dilation along the superior peripheral arcade of the right eye.  
11. The left eye had similar findings.

7. There was skin sloughing off the lesions on her elbows (Figure, B) and knees.
8. Four-millimeter punch biopsy specimens were taken from the left ear, right arm, and forehead (Figure, C and D).
9. Clinical and histopathologic images from a case of acral retiform purpura.
10. A, Dusky purpuric macules on the helical rim and antihelix of the ear.
11. B, Reticulated purpuric patches with focal areas of necrosis on the extensor surfaces of the arms.
12. C and D, In specimens from the forehead, multifocal intravascular fibrinoid material consisting of a mix of cryoglobulins and fibrin thrombi with relatively little vessel wall inflammation was seen (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×4 [C] and ×10 [D]).
